extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Santa Clara / general college-newspaper audience interested in media and journalism
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion piece assessing the ethical standards and public trust of broadcast news in light of the Brian Williams embellishment scandal; discusses what makes news trustworthy and what institutions/behaviors degrade that trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report the news fully, accurately, and fairly
rubrics_metrics.description: Gallup polls list Americans' 'confidence in the media’s ability to report ‘the news fully, accurately and fairly’' at a mere 40 percent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use completeness, accuracy, and fairness as core criteria when judging media; public confidence in media hinges on these qualities. The article cites declining Gallup poll numbers to indicate failure on these dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid embellishment and fabrication for ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Brian Williams embellished a 2003 helicopter crash in Iraq — an act the author calls 'merely good television' in a ratings-driven, sensationalist media environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not add or embellish details to make stories more dramatic. The piece treats embellishment as an ethical failing motivated by ratings and as a central reason for loss of trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prioritize ratings over journalistic integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Television is all about the ratings, and bringing in ratings while maintaining one’s journalistic integrity is difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news organizations on whether they put audience metrics above truthfulness; the author argues that sensationalism for ratings is a systemic cause of declining trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide oversight and correct mistakes promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: The KTVU fake passenger-names incident and Fox affiliates' delayed apology for a caption error demonstrate failures that 'could and should have easily been corrected with even the slightest bit of oversight.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A robust editorial/verification process that prevents obvious errors and enables fast corrections is a criterion for trustworthy outlets. Lapses in oversight are presented as evidence of media decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the substance, manner, and motives of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating 'the substance of the stories that media covers, the way they are covered and, most importantly, why they are covered' is crucial to restoring trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing media, consider (1) what topics are chosen, (2) how they are framed and reported, and (3) the incentives or motives driving coverage (e.g., ratings), not just surface errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold prominent anchors and journalists accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: The article discusses accountability (suspension, possible firing) for Brian Williams and notes that firing him alone will 'do very little to restore America’s trust in media' unless broader practices are addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountability for high-profile figures is a necessary criterion, but must be accompanied by institutional reforms; individual punishments without systemic change are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public-trust metrics as an indicator of media health
rubrics_metrics.description: References to historical Gallup trust levels (over 7 in 10 during Cronkite's era vs. 40 percent at time of writing) indicate using public opinion polling to measure media credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare current public-trust statistics to historical baselines to assess perceived legitimacy; declining poll numbers signal broader problems beyond isolated incidents.
